steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on forecasting vegetation from satellite imagery with deep learning. It should explain why fine-resolution vegetation forecasts matter, review existing approaches and datasets and their shortcomings, and introduce our new dataset and transformer model along with a list of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Why vegetation forecasting from satellite imagery matters
- Two existing lines of deep learning work and their limits
- EarthNet2021 and its weaknesses
- Our approach: GreenEarthNet dataset and the Contextformer model
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation
  - optical satellite images useful for monitoring vegetation status
  - applications: agricultural planning, forestry advisory, humanitarian assistance, carbon monitoring
  - prognostic info needed: farmers and weather scenarios (cite); humanitarian orgs, droughts and pastoral communities, famine mitigation with anticipatory action (cite); afforestation and future climate (cite)
  - hard: model must handle ecological memory effects (cite), spatial interactions, weather variations
  - deep nets good at relationships in space/time/modalities -> natural fit given big enough dataset
- Existing deep learning work: two groups
  - low-res global forecasting (cite): long-term AVHRR, MODIS records, coarse resolution
    - overlook within-pixel heterogeneity: grassland vs forest; neighbouring fields, winter wheat vs. maize; north-facing slope near river vs rocky south-facing slope under drought
  - high-res local satellite imagery forecasting (cite): field-scale heterogeneity, Sentinel 2 and Landsat, self-supervised
    - focus on perceptual image quality, not vegetation dynamics -> suitability uncertain
- EarthNet2021
  - largest dataset for high-res vegetation forecasting (cite) is EarthNet2021 (cite)
  - models can forecast images of high perceptual quality; unclear if this translates to vegetation dynamics
  - limits: faulty cloud mask, insufficient baselines, poorly interpretable evaluation
  - e.g. strong seasonal cycle -> vegetation climatology baseline needed, missing
- Our approach
  - continental-scale vegetation dynamics; predict greenness at 20m conditioned on coarse-scale weather
  - GreenEarthNet: Sentinel 2 red, green, blue, near-infrared; deep learning cloud mask; separate data corruption anomalies from meteorological/anthropogenic ones
  - same locations and spatial/temporal dims as EarthNet2021 -> reuse ConvLSTM (cite), SGED-ConvLSTM (cite), Earthformer (cite) as baselines
  - complete remake of EarthNet2021, removes weaknesses, enables self-supervised learning
  - Contextformer: light-weight transformer; Pyramid Vision Transformer backbone (cite) + local context patches; temporal transformer encoder conditioned on meteorology; delta-prediction from initial gap filled observation (persistence prior)
  - Fig. 1: \hat{V} from X, C, E via f
- Contributions
  - (1) GreenEarthNet: first large-scale dataset for within-year vegetation dynamics, learned cloud mask, new evaluation scheme
  - (2) Contextformer: multi-modal transformer, spatial context via vision backbone, temporal transformer on context patches
  - (3) comparison against unseen variety of SOTA models from related tasks; outperforms all across metrics

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Optical satellite images have proven to be useful for monitoring the status of vegetation. This is important for many applications in agricultural planning, forestry advisory, humanitarian assistance or carbon monitoring. In all of them prognostic information is relevant. Farmers want to know how their farmland may react to a given weather scenario. Humanitarian organisations need to understand the local impact of droughts on pastoral communities, so they can mitigate famine with anticipatory action. Afforestation efforts need to consider how their forests will react to future climate. But providing this prognostic information through fine resolution vegetation forecasts is challenging, because the model needs to consider ecological memory effects, spatial interactions and the influence of weather variations. Deep neural networks have been successful at modeling relationships in space, time or across modalities. So it seems natural to apply them to vegetation forecasting, given a dataset that is large enough.

Up to now, deep learning for vegetation forecasting can be roughly grouped into two categories: low-resolution global vegetation forecasting and high-resolution local satellite imagery forecasting. The first group builds on long-term measurements of vegetation status from the AVHRR and MODIS satellites, which have coarse resolution. These methods overlook the heterogeneity within each pixel. For example a grassland will react very differently than a forest, two neighbouring fields can have almost opposite dynamics depending on the type of crops (e.g. winter wheat vs. maize), and vegetation on a north-facing slope close to a river will generally react differently to drought stress than vegetation on a rocky south-facing slope. The second group instead tries to model the field-scale heterogeneity that is observed from the Sentinel 2 and Landsat satellites, using self-supervised learning. But so far these approaches have focused on perceptual image quality and not on vegetation dynamics, so it is uncertain if they are suitable for vegetation forecasting.

- EarthNet2021
  - largest dataset for high-res vegetation forecasting; good perceptual quality, unclear for vegetation dynamics
  - faulty cloud mask, insufficient baselines, poorly interpretable evaluation; no vegetation climatology baseline despite strong seasonal cycle
- Our approach
  - continental scale, greenness at 20m conditioned on coarse-scale weather
  - GreenEarthNet: Sentinel 2 red/green/blue/near-infrared, deep learning cloud mask (data corruption vs meteorological/anthropogenic anomalies)
  - consistent with EarthNet2021 -> ConvLSTM, SGED-ConvLSTM, Earthformer as baselines; complete remake, enables self-supervised learning
  - Contextformer: Pyramid Vision Transformer backbone + local context patches, temporal transformer encoder on meteorology, delta-prediction from gap filled observation
  - Fig. 1: \hat{V} from X, C, E via the Contextformer (f)
- Contributions
  - (1) GreenEarthNet dataset, learned cloud mask, new evaluation scheme
  - (2) Contextformer
  - (3) comparison against many SOTA models from related tasks, outperforms all

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Optical satellite images have proven to be useful for monitoring the status of vegetation. This is important for many applications in agricultural planning, forestry advisory, humanitarian assistance or carbon monitoring. In all of them prognostic information is relevant. Farmers want to know how their farmland may react to a given weather scenario. Humanitarian organisations need to understand the local impact of droughts on pastoral communities, so they can mitigate famine with anticipatory action. Afforestation efforts need to consider how their forests will react to future climate. But providing this prognostic information through fine resolution vegetation forecasts is challenging, because the model needs to consider ecological memory effects, spatial interactions and the influence of weather variations. Deep neural networks have been successful at modeling relationships in space, time or across modalities. So it seems natural to apply them to vegetation forecasting, given a dataset that is large enough.

Up to now, deep learning for vegetation forecasting can be roughly grouped into two categories: low-resolution global vegetation forecasting and high-resolution local satellite imagery forecasting. The first group builds on long-term measurements of vegetation status from the AVHRR and MODIS satellites, which have coarse resolution. These methods overlook the heterogeneity within each pixel. For example a grassland will react very differently than a forest, two neighbouring fields can have almost opposite dynamics depending on the type of crops (e.g. winter wheat vs. maize), and vegetation on a north-facing slope close to a river will generally react differently to drought stress than vegetation on a rocky south-facing slope. The second group instead tries to model the field-scale heterogeneity that is observed from the Sentinel 2 and Landsat satellites, using self-supervised learning. But so far these approaches have focused on perceptual image quality and not on vegetation dynamics, so it is uncertain if they are suitable for vegetation forecasting.

The largest dataset for high resolution vegetation forecasting is EarthNet2021. In theory, a model trained on EarthNet2021 can forecast satellite images with high perceptual quality. But it is harder to assess whether this skill also carries over to predicting derived vegetation dynamics. Here EarthNet2021 is limited by a faulty cloud mask, insufficient baselines and an evaluation protocol that is hard to interpret. For example, natural vegetation follows a strong seasonal cycle, so a vegetation climatology is a necessary baseline to compare with, and EarthNet2021 does not have one.

In this paper we approach modeling vegetation dynamics at continental scale. We do this by predicting remotely sensed vegetation greenness at 20m, conditioned on coarse-scale weather. For this we introduce the GreenEarthNet dataset. It includes the Sentinel 2 bands red, green, blue and near-infrared and a high quality cloud mask based on deep learning, which makes it possible to tell apart anomalies that come from data corruption and anomalies that come from meteorological and anthropogenic influence. We keep the training locations and the spatial and temporal dimensions of GreenEarthNet consistent with EarthNet2021, so the leading models ConvLSTM, SGED-ConvLSTM and Earthformer can be re-used as baselines for vegetation forecasting. So GreenEarthNet is a complete remake of EarthNet2021 that removes all its weaknesses and enables self-supervised learning for geospatial vegetation forecasting. To advance the state-of-the-art on the new dataset we present a light-weight transformer model, the Contextformer. It uses a Pyramid Vision Transformer as the vision backbone and local context patches to make use of spatial interactions. Then it models the temporal dynamics conditioned on coarse-scale meteorology with a temporal transformer encoder. Finally it puts a strong prior on persistence with a delta-prediction scheme that starts from an initial, gap filled observation. Fig. 1 shows a sketch of our GreenEarthNet approach: the future vegetation state (\hat{V}) is predicted from past satellite image spectra (X), past and future weather data (C), and elevation information (E) with a deep neural network, the Contextformer (f).

Our main contributions are the following. (1) We present the GreenEarthNet dataset, which is the first large-scale dataset suitable for predicting within-year vegetation dynamics, and it includes a learned cloud mask and a new evaluation scheme. (2) We introduce the Contextformer, a new multi-modal transformer model for vegetation forecasting, which uses spatial context through its vision backbone and forecasts the temporal evolution of small context patches with a temporal transformer. (3) We compare the Contextformer against a variety of state-of-the-art models from related tasks that has not been seen before, and we find it outperforms all of them across metrics.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Optical satellite images have proven useful for monitoring vegetation status. This is essential for a variety of applications in agricultural planning, forestry advisory, humanitarian assistance or carbon monitoring. In all these cases, prognostic information is relevant: Farmers want to know how their farmland may react to a given weather scenario [1]. Humanitarian organisations need to understand the localized impact of droughts on pastoral communities to mitigate famine with anticipatory action [2]. Afforestation efforts need to consider how their forests will react to future climate [3]. However, providing such prognostic information through fine resolution vegetation forecasts is challenging, as it requires a model that considers ecological memory effects [4], spatial interactions and the influence of weather variations. Deep neural networks have proven successful at modeling relationships in space, time or across modalities. Hence, applying them to vegetation forecasting given a sufficiently large dataset seems natural.

So far, deep learning for vegetation forecasting can be roughly grouped into two categories: low-resolution global vegetation forecasting and high-resolution local satellite imagery forecasting. The former [5,4,6,7,8,9,10] builds upon long-term measurements of vegetation status from the coarse resolution AVHRR and MODIS satellites. These methods overlook the heterogeneity within each pixel: a grassland will react very differently than a forest, two neighbouring fields can have almost opposite dynamics depending on the type of crops (e.g. winter wheat vs. maize), and vegetation on a north-facing slope close to a river will generally react differently to drought stress than on a rocky south-facing slope. The latter [11,12,13,14,15,16], in contrast, aims at modeling the field-scale heterogeneity observed from the Sentinel 2 and Landsat satellites through self-supervised learning. However, these approaches have so far focused on perceptual image quality rather than vegetation dynamics, which makes their suitability for vegetation forecasting uncertain.

The largest dataset for high resolution vegetation forecasting [17] is EarthNet2021 [11]. In theory, a model trained on EarthNet2021 can forecast satellite images of high perceptual quality. It is, however, harder to assess whether this skill also translates to predicting derived vegetation dynamics. Here, the suitability of EarthNet2021 is limited by a faulty cloud mask, insufficient baselines and a poorly interpretable evaluation protocol. For instance, natural vegetation follows a strong seasonal cycle, which makes a vegetation climatology a necessary baseline to compare with, yet it is lacking on EarthNet2021.

In this paper, we approach continental-scale modeling of vegetation dynamics. To achieve this, we predict remotely sensed vegetation greenness at 20m conditioned on coarse-scale weather, and for this we introduce the GreenEarthNet dataset. It includes the Sentinel 2 bands red, green, blue and near-infrared and a high quality deep learning-based cloud mask, which allows distinguishing between anomalies due to data corruption and those due to meteorological and anthropogenic influence. The training locations and spatial and temporal dimensions of GreenEarthNet are kept consistent with EarthNet2021, which enables re-using the leading models ConvLSTM [13], SGED-ConvLSTM [12] and Earthformer [18] as baselines for vegetation forecasting. In other words, GreenEarthNet is a complete remake of EarthNet2021 that removes all its weaknesses and enables self-supervised learning for geospatial vegetation forecasting. To advance the state-of-the-art on the new dataset, we present a light-weight transformer model, the Contextformer. It uses a Pyramid Vision Transformer [19,20] as vision backbone and local context patches to make use of spatial interactions. It then models temporal dynamics conditioned on coarse-scale meteorology with a temporal transformer encoder. Finally, it puts a strong prior on persistence through a delta-prediction scheme starting from an initial, gap filled observation. Fig. 1 sketches our GreenEarthNet approach: Future vegetation state (\hat{V}) is predicted from past satellite image spectra (X), past and future weather data (C), and elevation information (E) via a deep neural network, the Contextformer (f).

Our major contributions can be summarized as follows. (1) We present the GreenEarthNet dataset, the first large-scale dataset suitable for prediction of within-year vegetation dynamics, including a learned cloud mask and a new evaluation scheme. (2) We introduce the Contextformer, a novel multi-modal transformer model for vegetation forecasting that leverages spatial context through its vision backbone and forecasts the temporal evolution of small context patches with a temporal transformer. (3) We compare the Contextformer against a previously unseen variety of state-of-the-art models from related tasks and find that it outperforms all of them across metrics.
